messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 76

He is a 25-year-old African man who works as a journalist, and when he first starts talking about what happened, he does so carefully, as if choosing each word might keep the memory at a safe distance. Before the event, he describes himself as driven and curious, the kind of person who likes being in the middle of things, asking questions other people avoid, especially in his work. He takes pride in reporting stories that matter, and he has built a life around moving toward what others turn away from. He is in a relationship, and he says his partner has often told him that his boldness is one of the things she admires most about him.

That sense of himself changes on the day he is confronted by police. He is covering a developing story when the situation turns chaotic. He remembers the noise first—the shouting, the sharp commands, the sudden rush of bodies and movement. The officers are not simply present; they become the center of danger. He feels trapped between his role as an observer and his immediate need to survive. He describes trying to show his press identification, trying to explain who he is and why he is there, but the moment unfolds too quickly for reason to matter. He is grabbed, pushed, frightened by how fast authority becomes threat. What stays with him most is the experience of powerlessness: the sense that no answer he gives can protect him, that his body is at the mercy of other people’s anger and control.

In the days after, he does not feel like the same person. He says he moves through his routines in a kind of suspended state, as if part of him remains at the scene while the rest of him attempts to function. He becomes hyperaware of uniforms, sirens, radios, and even the sight of a checkpoint in the distance. When he hears footsteps behind him or sees a vehicle with flashing lights, his chest tightens and his mind jumps back to the original moment of being seized. He notices himself scanning exits whenever he enters a room. He sits with his back to walls. He no longer enjoys being out in public, even though his work requires it, because being seen now feels dangerous in a way it never did before.

Sleep becomes disrupted. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes unrefreshed, often from dreams that are not exact repeats of the event but carry its same terror and helplessness. Some nights he wakes with his heart racing, unsure for a few seconds where he is. He says that in the quiet of the night, his mind brings him back to details he wishes it would leave alone: the tone of the officers’ voices, the sensation of being physically overpowered, the humiliation of being treated as if his identity meant nothing. During the day, those memories intrude without warning. A sound, a smell, a passing uniform can pull him out of the present. When this happens, he becomes tense and irritable, and he has to work hard not to show how shaken he is.

As a journalist, he cannot fully step away from the world that frightened him. He still follows news, attends events when he can, and tries to keep up appearances, but the work now comes with a layer of dread. He is more cautious with assignments, especially those involving public demonstrations, police presence, or politically tense settings. He says he used to go toward conflict because he believed reporting required courage, but now courage feels different; it feels like having to argue with his own body every time he leaves home with a notebook and recorder. He worries that fear is narrowing the life he once had.

In his relationship, he is more distant and more easily startled. His partner notices that he has become quieter, sometimes disappearing into his thoughts for long stretches. He tries not to burden her, but the effort to hide how much he is struggling leaves him feeling lonely. He also carries shame about that loneliness, as though he should be able to “move on” because nothing in him was physically broken in a lasting way. Yet he knows something has changed. He does not trust public spaces the way he used to, and he no longer feels fully safe in the presence of authority. Even now, he describes living with the sense that danger can appear suddenly and without warning, and that his body is always waiting for it.
